IFR-001.e: The Scheme sets the preparation, voluntary and mandatory stages for IFRS adoption.
o: The Scheme for applying IFRS in Vietnam
IFR-001.x:
Basis: Decision 345/QĐ-BTC of 16/03/2020.
Analysis: Decision 345 approved the Scheme for applying IFRS in Vietnam: preparation (2020–2021), voluntary (2022–2025), mandatory by group (after 2025), plus developing VFRS based on IFRS.
Distractors: B were issued 2001–2005; C is Circular 133/2016; D is Circular 214/2012.

IFR-002.q: Match each stage of the Scheme under Decision 345/QD-BTC with its timing:
IFR-002.e: Stage 2 implementation depends on subsequent guidance (e.g., Circular 118/2026/TT-BTC, the VFRS plan).
p: Stage 2 – mandatory for groups of entities
After 2025, as prescribed by the MOF
IFR-002.x:
Basis: Decision 345/QĐ-BTC.
Analysis: Preparation 2020–2021 (guidance, training, IFRS translation); phase 1 – voluntary 2022–2025; phase 2 – mandatory by group after 2025, per Ministry rules.
Note: Phase 2 depends on later texts (Circular 118/2026, the VFRS plan) – in practice Circular 118/2026 keeps IFRS voluntary (IFR-005).

IFR-003.q: Under Decision 345/QD-BTC, the voluntary stage mainly targets consolidated FS of entities such as parents of state economic groups, listed companies and large public companies.
IFR-003.e: True. Other enterprises may voluntarily apply it to separate FS if they have the need and resources.
IFR-003.x:
Basis: Decision 345/QĐ-BTC.
Analysis: True. The voluntary phase targets mainly consolidated FS of State group parents, listed companies, large public companies and foreign-invested parents with the need and resources; others may voluntarily apply it to separate FS.

o: The subjects, scope and manner of applying IFRS in Vietnam
IFR-004.x:
Basis: Circular 118/2026/TT-BTC (per the question's source).
Analysis: Circular 118/2026 sets who may apply IFRS in Vietnam, the scope and procedures, effective 01/01/2027 (ACC-081).
Distractors: B, C and D belong to other texts.
Note: It post-dates the assistant's knowledge; check the original.

IFR-005.q: Under Circular 118/2026/TT-BTC, an enterprise's application of IFRS is voluntary.
IFR-005.e: True. Enterprises assess their needs and resources and notify the MOF before applying.
IFR-005.x:
Basis: Circular 118/2026/TT-BTC (per the question's source).
Analysis: True. IFRS adoption is voluntary: businesses assess their needs (investors, banks, foreign parents) and resources (people, systems), notify the Ministry beforehand (IFR-007) and apply IFRS unmodified (ACC-083).

IFR-006.q: When preparing IFRS FS for the first time, an entity applies:
IFR-006.e: IFRS 1 sets the transition date, optional exemptions and mandatory exceptions.
IFR-006.x:
Basis: IFRS 1 – First-time adoption; Circular 118/2026/TT-BTC.
Analysis: First IFRS FS apply IFRS 1: set the transition date (IFR-017), prepare an opening IFRS statement of financial position, apply IFRS retrospectively subject to optional exemptions and mandatory exceptions, and present reconciliations.
Distractors: IAS 8 covers policy changes once on IFRS; IFRS 18 and IAS 1 are presentation standards.

IFR-007.q: Under Circular 118/2026/TT-BTC, a decision to start or stop applying IFRS takes effect from:
IFR-007.e: This ensures consistency throughout the financial year.
o: The beginning of the next financial year, after notifying the MOF at least 30 days ahead
IFR-007.x:
Basis: Circular 118/2026/TT-BTC (per the question's source).
Analysis: Businesses notify the Ministry at least 30 days ahead; starting or stopping IFRS takes effect from the next financial year – keeping one consistent framework for the whole year (ACC-082).
Distractors: B and C break in-year consistency; D has no basis.

IFR-008.q: Under the plan announced on 13/10/2026, the Vietnamese Financial Reporting Standards (VFRS) are expected to comprise:
IFR-008.e: VFRS are to be issued in several batches through 2029.
IFR-008.x:
Basis: VFRS plan announced 13/10/2026 (per the question's source).
Analysis: VFRS is planned as 42 standards based on IFRS (2026 edition), issued in waves to 2029 (10 – 21 – 11, ACC-084).
Distractors: B is the current VAS count; C is only wave 1; D – Vietnam doesn't use US GAAP.

IFR-009.q: Under the plan announced in October 2026, VFRS are expected to become mandatory from 01/01/2031.
IFR-009.e: True (expected). It is a plan; watch for the official legal text.
IFR-009.x:
Basis: VFRS plan (13/10/2026) (per the question's source).
Analysis: True (planned). Once all 42 standards are done, the Ministry expects a circular mandating them from 01/01/2031 (ACC-085).
Note: It's a plan and may change – watch for the official text.

IFR-010.q: Select ALL main benefits of IFRS adoption for Vietnamese enterprises:
IFR-010.e: Accounting standards do not determine tax; tax follows tax law.
o: Better ability to attract foreign investment
Higher information quality, supporting market upgrade
IFR-010.x:
Basis: Decision 345/QĐ-BTC (Scheme objectives).
Analysis: Benefits: (A) attracting foreign capital – investors read a common reporting language; (B) comparability with international peers; (C) better quality, transparency, supporting market upgrades.
Distractors: (D) CIT follows tax law, not accounting standards – differences are adjusted in the tax return.

IFR-011.q: Select ALL correct differences between current VAS and IFRS:
IFR-011.e: Vietnam uses overdue-age receivable provisions (Circular 48/2019), not ECL.
o: VAS has no standard equivalent to IAS 36 on impairment
VAS has no biological assets standard equivalent to IAS 41
VAS 06 keeps lessees' operating leases off balance sheet
VAS requires expected credit loss (ECL) provisioning like IFRS 9
IFR-011.x:
Basis: VAS; IFRS (IAS 36, IAS 41, IFRS 16, IFRS 9); Circular 48/2019/TT-BTC.
Analysis: Correct differences: (A) no VAS equivalent of IAS 36 – impairment; (B) none for IAS 41 – agriculture (Circular 99 only adds account 215); (C) VAS 06 keeps lessees' operating leases off balance sheet (ACC-095).
Distractors: (D) Vietnam provisions receivables by overdue period (Circular 48/2019), not IFRS 9's expected credit loss model.

IFR-012.q: Under Vietnamese consolidation rules, goodwill is amortised (up to 10 years), whereas under IFRS goodwill is not amortised but tested annually for impairment.
IFR-012.e: True. This major difference affects profit on transition.
IFR-012.x:
Basis: Circular 202/2014/TT-BTC (consolidation); IFRS 3; IAS 36.
Analysis: True. Vietnamese rules amortise goodwill over at most 10 years. Under IFRS 3, goodwill isn't amortised but tested for impairment at least annually under IAS 36 (cash-generating units).
Note: On conversion profit may rise (no amortisation) but become more volatile (one-off impairment charges).

IFR-013.q: IFRS Accounting Standards are issued by:
IFR-013.e: IAASB issues auditing standards; FASB issues US GAAP.
o: The IASB of the IFRS Foundation
IFR-013.x:
Basis: IFRS Foundation (governance structure).
Analysis: IFRS Accounting Standards are issued by the IASB (International Accounting Standards Board) under the IFRS Foundation.
Distractors: IFAC – International Federation of Accountants (home of IAASB, IESBA); FASB – US GAAP; IAASB – ISAs.

IFR-014.q: The role of the IFRS Interpretations Committee is to:
IFR-014.e: Agenda decisions carry explanatory weight in practice.
o: Support the IASB on application issues, issue interpretations (IFRIC) and agenda decisions
IFR-014.x:
Basis: IFRS Foundation – IFRS Interpretations Committee.
Analysis: The Committee supports the IASB on application issues: issuing IFRIC interpretations (ratified by the IASB, mandatory) and agenda decisions – explaining how existing standards apply, highly persuasive in practice.
Distractors: B – auditors; C – tax authorities; D – securities regulators.

IFR-015.q: The ISSB, also under the IFRS Foundation, issues sustainability disclosure standards IFRS S1 and IFRS S2.
IFR-015.e: True. IFRS S2 focuses on climate-related disclosures.
IFR-015.x:
Basis: IFRS Foundation – ISSB (formed November 2021).
Analysis: True. The ISSB (International Sustainability Standards Board) under the IFRS Foundation issued IFRS S1 (general sustainability-related financial disclosures) and IFRS S2 (climate-related disclosures) in June 2023, effective for periods from 01/01/2024 – adoption depends on each jurisdiction.

IFR-016.q: Match each standard with its topic:
IFR-016.e: IFRS 18 is an Accounting Standard; S1 and S2 are Sustainability Disclosure Standards.
p: General requirements for sustainability-related financial disclosures
Presentation and disclosure in financial statements
IFR-016.x:
Basis: IFRS Foundation.
Analysis: IFRS S1 – general sustainability-related financial disclosures; IFRS S2 – climate-related disclosures (physical and transition risks, Scope 1–3 emissions); IFRS 18 – presentation and disclosure in FS (replacing IAS 1). S1 and S2 are Sustainability Disclosure Standards; IFRS 18 is an Accounting Standard.

IFR-017.q: An entity's first IFRS FS are for 2027 with one comparative year. The date of transition under IFRS 1 is:
IFR-017.e: The transition date is the start of the earliest comparative period; an opening IFRS statement of financial position is prepared at that date.
IFR-017.x:
Basis: IFRS 1.
Analysis: The transition date is the start of the earliest period presented with full IFRS comparatives. First IFRS FS for 2027 with one comparative year (2026) → transition date 01/01/2026, when the opening IFRS statement of financial position is prepared.
Distractors: B is the start of the reporting year; C is the reporting date; D is wrong – the date follows the rule, not choice.

IFR-018.q: IFRS 1 allows optional exemptions such as using fair value at the transition date as deemed cost for property, plant and equipment.
IFR-018.e: True. Conversely, estimates are a mandatory exception; hindsight may not be used.
IFR-018.x:
Basis: IFRS 1 (optional exemptions – Appendix D; mandatory exceptions – Appendix B).
Analysis: True. Entities may use fair value at the transition date as deemed cost for PP&E – avoiding reconstructing years of cost and depreciation history. By contrast, estimates are a mandatory exception: IFRS estimates at transition must be consistent with prior ones, without hindsight.

IFR-019.q: IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements is effective for annual periods beginning on or after:
IFR-019.e: Early application is permitted; it applies retrospectively.
IFR-019.x:
Basis: IFRS 18 – Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements (issued April 2024).
Analysis: IFRS 18 is effective for annual periods beginning on or after 01/01/2027; early application is permitted; it applies retrospectively (IFR-039).
Distractors: B, C and D aren't the effective date.

IFR-020.x:
Basis: IFRS 18.
Analysis: IFRS 18 replaces IAS 1 – Presentation of FS; many general IAS 1 requirements move into IFRS 18 or IAS 8. IAS 7 is amended alongside (indirect-method starting point, interest and dividend classification – IFR-024, IFR-025), not replaced.
Distractors: B is amended; C and D remain.

IFR-021.q: Under IFRS 18 (non-financial entity), match each item with its category in the statement of profit or loss:
IFR-021.e: IFRS 18 also has a discontinued operations category.
p: Revenue, cost of sales, selling expenses
Share of profit of associates under the equity method
IFR-021.x:
Basis: IFRS 18 (P&L categories – non-financial entities without a main business of investing or financing).
Analysis: Revenue, COGS, selling costs → operating (the default category); share of associates' profit under the equity method → investing; interest expense → financing; CIT expense → income taxes. There's also discontinued operations.

IFR-022.q: The two new mandatory subtotals under IFRS 18 are:
IFR-022.e: EBITDA is not mandatory; if presented it may be a management-defined performance measure.
o: Operating profit, and Profit before financing and income taxes
Net revenue and cost of sales
IFR-022.x:
Basis: IFRS 18.
Analysis: Two new mandatory subtotals: operating profit and profit before financing and income taxes – alongside profit or loss.
Distractors: B – EBITDA isn't required; if shown it's usually a management-defined measure (IFR-023); C and D aren't IFRS 18's new subtotals.

IFR-023.q: IFRS 18 requires management-defined performance measures (MPMs) to be disclosed in a single note with a reconciliation to the most directly comparable IFRS subtotal.
IFR-023.e: True. MPMs come within the audit scope, improving transparency of 'adjusted profit'.
IFR-023.x:
Basis: IFRS 18 (management-defined performance measures – MPMs).
Analysis: True. MPMs (e.g., 'adjusted profit', 'adjusted EBITDA' used in public communications) go in a single note: description, why useful, reconciliation to the closest IFRS subtotal, tax and NCI effects of each adjustment. Being in the FS, they fall within the audit.

IFR-024.q: Under IAS 7 as amended by IFRS 18, the starting point of the indirect method for operating cash flows is:
IFR-024.e: The change improves consistency between profit or loss and cash flows.
IFR-024.x:
Basis: IAS 7 as amended by IFRS 18.
Analysis: The indirect method starts from operating profit rather than profit before or after tax – linking the P&L directly to operating cash flow and removing diversity in practice.
Distractors: B and C were the old (optional) starting points; D isn't an indirect-method start.

IFR-025.q: Under the IAS 7 amendments accompanying IFRS 18, non-financial entities classify interest paid as financing and dividends and interest received as investing.
IFR-025.e: True. Removing previous choices improves comparability.
IFR-025.x:
Basis: IAS 7 as amended by IFRS 18.
Analysis: True. For non-financial entities (no main business of investing/financing): interest paid → financing; dividends and interest received → investing. The former classification choice (e.g., operating) is removed to improve comparability.

IFR-026.q: Select ALL components of a complete set of IFRS FS:
IFR-026.e: Internal management reports are not part of the FS; segment information (IFRS 8) appears in the notes.
o: Statement(s) of financial performance (profit or loss and OCI)
Detailed internal management reports by segment
IFR-026.x:
Basis: IFRS 18 (formerly IAS 1).
Analysis: A complete set: (A) statement of financial position; (B) statement(s) of financial performance (P&L and OCI); (C) statement of changes in equity; (D) cash flow statement; (E) notes – with comparatives.
Distractors: (F) Internal management reports aren't FS; IFRS 8 segment data sits in the notes.
Note: Unlike VAS, IFRS has a separate statement of changes in equity and OCI.

IFR-027.q: Under the Conceptual Framework (2018), the two fundamental qualitative characteristics of useful financial information are:
IFR-027.e: Comparability, verifiability, timeliness and understandability are enhancing characteristics.
IFR-027.x:
Basis: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting (IASB, 2018) – Chapter 2.
Analysis: Two fundamental qualitative characteristics: relevance (predictive and confirmatory value; materiality) and faithful representation (complete, neutral, free from error).
Distractors: B and C are enhancing characteristics (with comparability and verifiability – IFR-028); D are VAS 01 principles, not fundamental characteristics under the IFRS Framework.

IFR-028.q: Match each enhancing qualitative characteristic with its content:
IFR-028.e: Enhancing characteristics add usefulness but cannot rescue irrelevant or unfaithful information.
p: Identifying similarities and differences across items, periods, entities
Independent observers could reach consensus on faithful representation
Information available in time to influence decisions
Clear, concise classification, characterisation and presentation
IFR-028.x:
Basis: Conceptual Framework (2018).
Analysis: Comparability – identifying similarities and differences across items, periods and entities; verifiability – knowledgeable independent observers could reach consensus; timeliness – available while it can influence decisions; understandability – clear, concise classification, description and presentation.
Note: Enhancing characteristics can't make irrelevant or unfaithful information useful.

IFR-029.q: Under the Conceptual Framework (2018), an asset is:
IFR-029.e: An economic resource is a right with the potential to produce economic benefits; certainty is not required.
o: A present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events
Future economic benefits certain to be received
IFR-029.x:
Basis: Conceptual Framework (2018) – Chapter 4.
Analysis: An asset is a present economic resource controlled by the entity as a result of past events; an economic resource is a right with the potential to produce economic benefits – no 'certain' or 'probable' requirement as in 2010.
Distractors: B – control, not necessarily legal ownership (e.g., leased right-of-use assets); C wrongly stresses certainty; D – spending isn't the same as an asset.

IFR-030.q: Under the Conceptual Framework (2018), prudence is caution when making judgements under uncertainty and supports neutrality; it does not permit deliberate understatement of assets.
IFR-030.e: True. Prudence is not systematic bias.
IFR-030.x:
Basis: Conceptual Framework (2018), paragraph 2.16.
Analysis: True. The 2018 Framework reintroduces 'prudence' as caution in judgments under uncertainty, supporting neutrality – not overstating assets or income, but also not deliberately understating assets or income or overstating liabilities or expenses. This differs from the asymmetric prudence often read into VAS 01.

IFR-031.q: Under IAS 8, a voluntary change in accounting policy is applied:
IFR-031.e: Adjust opening balances of the earliest period presented.
IFR-031.x:
Basis: IAS 8 – Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors.
Analysis: A voluntary policy change (for more reliable, relevant information) is applied retrospectively – adjusting opening balances of the earliest period presented and comparatives – unless impracticable.
Distractors: B and C apply to estimate changes; D – it isn't optional.

IFR-032.q: A change in the estimated useful life of PP&E is treated:
IFR-032.e: The effect is recognised in current and future periods.
o: Prospectively – it is a change in accounting estimate
IFR-032.x:
Basis: IAS 8; IAS 16 (reviewing useful lives).
Analysis: Useful life is an accounting estimate; changes are prospective – affecting the current and future periods (carrying amount spread over the remaining life), with no restatement.
Distractors: B and C apply to policy changes and error corrections; D is wrong.

IFR-033.q: Material prior-period errors are corrected retrospectively by restating comparatives.
IFR-033.x:
Basis: IAS 8.
Analysis: True. Material prior-period errors are corrected retrospectively in the first FS approved after discovery: restating comparatives for the period of the error, or opening balances of the earliest period presented if earlier. They aren't corrected through current-period profit or loss.

IFR-034.q: Under IAS 10, which is an ADJUSTING event?
IFR-034.e: The ruling provides evidence of an obligation existing at period end.
o: Settlement after period end of a court case existing at period end
A sharp fall in share prices after period end
A plant fire after period end
Announcement of a merger after period end
IFR-034.x:
Basis: IAS 10 – Events after the reporting period.
Analysis: Adjusting events provide evidence of conditions existing at the period end – a ruling on an existing lawsuit confirms a present obligation at that date (as in VAS 23, ACC-034).
Distractors: B, C and D are conditions arising after the period end → non-adjusting, disclosed if material.

IFR-035.q: Dividends declared after the reporting period are not recognised as a liability at the reporting date.
IFR-035.x:
Basis: IAS 10.
Analysis: True. Dividends declared after the period end aren't a present obligation at that date (no decision yet), so no liability is recognised; they're only disclosed.

IFR-036.q: Management intends to liquidate the entity. Under IFRS, the FS:
IFR-036.e: Another basis (e.g., liquidation) must be used and disclosed.
o: Cannot be prepared on a going concern basis
Are still on a going concern basis with disclosure
IFR-036.x:
Basis: IFRS 18 (formerly IAS 1, going concern); IAS 10.
Analysis: If management intends to liquidate or cease trading, or has no realistic alternative, FS can't be prepared on a going-concern basis; another basis (e.g., liquidation) is used and disclosed. Under IAS 10, even if the intent arises after the period end, the going-concern basis becomes inappropriate.
Distractors: B breaches the standard (cf. VSA-100); C and D are wrong.

IFR-037.q: Under IFRS 18 (non-financial entity): revenue 1,000; cost of sales 600; selling and admin 200; share of associates' profit (equity method) 30; interest expense 40 (VND billion). What is operating profit (VND billion)?
IFR-037.e: 1,000 − 600 − 200 = 200; associates' share is investing; interest is financing.
IFR-037.x:
Basis: IFRS 18.
Working: Operating profit = revenue 1,000 − COGS 600 − selling and admin 200 = 200 billion VND. Associate income (30) is investing and interest (40) financing → excluded from operating profit.

IFR-038.q: Under IFRS 18 (non-financial entity): revenue 1,000; cost of sales 600; selling and admin 200; share of associate profit (equity method) 30; interest expense 40 (VND billion). What is profit before financing and income taxes (VND billion)?
IFR-038.x:
Basis: IFRS 18.
Working: Profit before financing and income taxes = operating profit 200 + investing 30 = 230 billion VND. Profit before tax = 230 − interest 40 = 190 billion.

IFR-039.q: IFRS 18 applies retrospectively; comparatives must be restated in the new structure.
IFR-039.e: True. Entities need 2026 data in the IFRS 18 structure.
IFR-039.x:
Basis: IFRS 18 (transition).
Analysis: True. IFRS 18 applies retrospectively under IAS 8: comparatives must be restated in the new structure (categories, subtotals, MPMs). So adopters from 2027 must prepare 2026 data in the IFRS 18 format, including reconciliations at initial application.

IFR-040.q: Select ALL items recognised in other comprehensive income (OCI):
IFR-040.e: FVTPL gains and losses go to profit or loss.
o: Revaluation surplus on PP&E under the revaluation model
Exchange differences on translating foreign operations
Gains on financial assets at FVTPL
IFR-040.x:
Basis: IAS 16; IAS 21; IAS 19; IFRS 9.
Analysis: Recognised in OCI: (A) revaluation surplus on PP&E under the revaluation model (IAS 16); (B) exchange differences on translating foreign operations (IAS 21); (C) remeasurements of defined benefit obligations (IAS 19).
Distractors: (D) Gains/losses on FVTPL financial assets go to profit or loss – as the name says.

IFR-041.q: IFRS 18 changes revenue recognition and measurement principles.
IFR-041.e: False. IFRS 18 changes only presentation and disclosure; revenue recognition stays under IFRS 15.
IFR-041.x:
Basis: IFRS 18; IFRS 15.
Analysis: False. IFRS 18 changes only presentation and disclosure (P&L structure, subtotals, MPMs, aggregation and disaggregation), not recognition or measurement. Revenue recognition remains under IFRS 15 (five-step model – IFR-043).

IFR-042.e: Diluted EPS also adjusts for potential ordinary shares.
o: Profit attributable to ordinary equity holders of the parent / weighted average ordinary shares outstanding
IFR-042.x:
Basis: IAS 33 – Earnings per share.
Analysis: Basic EPS = profit attributable to the parent's ordinary shareholders / weighted average ordinary shares outstanding (as in VAS 30 – ACC-129). Diluted EPS adjusts for potential ordinary shares (convertibles, options).
Distractors: B, C and D are other ratios.

IFR-043.e: The model applies to all customer contracts within IFRS 15's scope.
o: Identify the contract with a customer
Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations
Recognise revenue when (or as) obligations are satisfied
IFR-043.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 – Revenue from Contracts with Customers.
Analysis: Five steps: (1) identify the contract; (2) identify performance obligations; (3) determine the transaction price; (4) allocate it to the obligations; (5) recognise revenue when (or as) each is satisfied. Logic: know the obligations and total price before allocating, then recognise per obligation.

IFR-044.e: Identifying obligations correctly drives the timing and amount of revenue.
o: A promise to transfer a distinct good/service (or a series of substantially the same distinct goods/services) to the customer
IFR-044.x:
Basis: IFRS 15.
Analysis: A performance obligation is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service (IFR-045), or a series of substantially the same distinct goods or services with the same pattern of transfer (e.g., daily cleaning). Identifying them correctly drives timing and amount of revenue.
Distractors: B is too broad (payment and penalty terms aren't performance obligations); C and D are other obligations.

IFR-045.q: A good/service is distinct when the customer can benefit from it (alone or with readily available resources) and the promise is separately identifiable in the contract.
IFR-045.e: True. Both criteria must be met.
IFR-045.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraph 27.
Analysis: True. A good or service is distinct if both: (1) capable of being distinct – the customer benefits on its own or with readily available resources; (2) distinct in the contract context – separately identifiable (not significantly integrated, modified, or highly interdependent). E.g., materials and labour integrated into a building form one obligation.

IFR-046.q: A bundle priced at 12,000: a machine (standalone price 10,000) and maintenance (standalone price 5,000). How much revenue is allocated to the machine?
IFR-046.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 (allocation by relative standalone selling price).
Working: Total standalone prices = 10,000 + 5,000 = 15,000; bundle discount = 3,000 (20%). Machine = 12,000 × 10,000 / 15,000 = 8,000 (recognised on delivery).
Check: 8,000 + 4,000 (IFR-047) = 12,000.

IFR-047.q: A bundle priced at 12,000 includes a machine (standalone price 10,000) and maintenance (standalone price 5,000). How much revenue is allocated to maintenance?
IFR-047.x:
Basis: IFRS 15.
Working: Maintenance = 12,000 × 5,000 / 15,000 = 4,000; recognised over the service period (e.g., 2 years → 2,000 a year).
Note: The bundle discount is allocated proportionately unless observable evidence shows it relates to only some obligations.

IFR-048.q: Under IFRS 15, variable consideration is estimated using:
IFR-048.e: Choose the method that best predicts the amount of entitlement.
o: The expected value or the most likely amount
IFR-048.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraph 53.
Analysis: Two methods for variable consideration: expected value (sum of probability × outcome – suits many similar contracts, many outcomes) or most likely amount (suits two outcomes, like a bonus achieved or not). Use whichever predicts best, consistently.
Distractors: B, C and D have no basis.

IFR-049.q: Variable consideration is included in the transaction price only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue will not occur.
IFR-049.e: True. This is the constraint on variable consideration.
IFR-049.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraph 56 (the constraint).
Analysis: True. Variable consideration is included only to the extent it is highly probable that a significant reversal of cumulative revenue won't occur when the uncertainty resolves – avoiding booking then reversing. Reversal risk rises with factors outside control, limited experience and many possible outcomes.

IFR-050.q: A contract has an early-completion bonus of VND 100 million: 60% probability of earning it, 40% not. Under the expected value method, what is the estimated bonus (VND million, before the constraint)?
IFR-050.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 (expected value method).
Working: 60% × 100 + 40% × 0 = 60 million VND.
Note: With just two outcomes, the most likely amount (100 million) usually predicts better; the constraint (IFR-049) still applies – 60% may not be 'highly probable' enough to include it all.

IFR-051.q: Which criterion allows revenue to be recognised over time?
IFR-051.e: Other criteria: customer controls the asset as created; no alternative use plus an enforceable right to payment for work done.
o: The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs
The customer has signed a contract
The customer has paid a deposit
IFR-051.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraph 35.
Analysis: Revenue is recognised over time if any of three criteria holds: (A) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits as performed (cleaning, security); the customer controls the asset as it's created (building on customer land); the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work done.
Distractors: B, C and D don't transfer control.

IFR-052.q: A construction contract priced at 1,500 billion with total expected costs of 1,000 billion; cumulative costs incurred 300 billion (input method). What cumulative revenue is recognised (VND billion)?
IFR-052.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 (input method for measuring progress).
Working: Progress = 300 / 1,000 = 30%. Cumulative revenue = 30% × 1,500 = 450 billion VND; cumulative gross profit = 450 − 300 = 150 billion (matching the expected margin 500/1,500 = 33.3%).
Note: Exclude costs that don't depict progress (abnormal waste, uninstalled materials).

IFR-053.q: An entity acting as an agent under IFRS 15 recognises revenue:
IFR-053.e: A principal controlling goods before transfer records gross revenue.
o: At the gross price charged to customers
IFR-053.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 (principal versus agent).
Analysis: An agent doesn't control the good or service before transfer → recognises revenue net – its commission or fee. A principal (controls before transfer: primary responsibility for fulfilment, inventory risk, pricing discretion) → recognises gross.
Distractors: B applies to principals; C and D are wrong.

IFR-054.q: An e-commerce platform (agent) processes VND 1,000 billion of sellers' sales and earns 8% commission. What is the platform's revenue (VND billion)?
IFR-054.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 (agents recognise net).
Working: Platform revenue = 1,000 × 8% = 80 billion VND. The 1,000 billion GMV isn't the platform's revenue.
Note: Distinguish GMV (an operating metric) from accounting revenue – investors often confuse them when reading e-commerce platforms' reports.

IFR-055.q: Incremental costs of obtaining a contract (e.g., sales commissions) are capitalised if expected to be recovered; they may be expensed if the amortisation period is one year or less (practical expedient).
IFR-055.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraphs 91–94.
Analysis: True. Incremental costs of obtaining a contract (incurred only if it's won – like sales commissions) are capitalised if expected to be recovered, amortised in line with the related transfer. Practical expedient: if amortisation would be 1 year or less, expense them.
Note: Costs incurred regardless of winning (general legal fees) aren't incremental.

IFR-056.q: A supermarket sells goods for 95,000 (VND thousand) and grants loyalty points with an estimated standalone price of 5,000; the goods' standalone price is 95,000. How much revenue is allocated to the points (recognised on redemption) (VND thousand)?
IFR-056.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 (customer options – loyalty points as a material right).
Working: Points = 95,000 × 5,000 / (95,000 + 5,000) = 4,750 thousand VND (a contract liability, recognised when redeemed or expired). Goods revenue = 95,000 − 4,750 = 90,250 thousand VND.

IFR-057.q: A significant financing component must be adjusted for when:
IFR-057.e: The transaction price reflects the cash selling price at transfer.
o: The gap between payment and transfer exceeds one year with a significant financing benefit (no adjustment needed if one year or less)
IFR-057.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraphs 60–65.
Analysis: Adjust for a significant financing component when payment timing gives either party a significant financing benefit; practical expedient: no adjustment if payment and transfer are within 1 year. The transaction price reflects the cash selling price at transfer; the difference is interest income or expense.
Distractors: B is too broad; C and D are wrong.

IFR-058.q: Under a bill-and-hold arrangement, revenue may be recognised before delivery if: there is a substantive reason, goods are identified as the customer's, ready for delivery and cannot be directed to another customer.
IFR-058.e: True. This exception must be strictly evidenced.
IFR-058.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, Appendix B (B79–B82 – bill-and-hold).
Analysis: True. Besides general control-transfer indicators, all four must hold: a substantive reason (usually the customer's request); goods separately identified as the customer's; ready for delivery; unusable for or transferable to other customers. It's a high revenue-fraud-risk area requiring strong evidence.

IFR-059.q: An assurance-type warranty (only assuring the product meets specifications) is accounted for:
IFR-059.e: A service-type warranty (beyond assurance, sold separately) is a separate performance obligation.
IFR-059.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, Appendix B (B28–B33); IAS 37.
Analysis: Assurance-type warranties – only promising the product meets specifications – aren't a separate service → accounted as an IAS 37 provision (estimated cost recognised at sale).
Distractors: B applies to service-type warranties (beyond assurance, sellable separately); C and D are wrong.

IFR-060.q: Match each contract item with its IFRS 15 accounting:
p: Separate performance obligation, revenue over time
Refund liability and an asset for the right to recover goods
IFR-060.x:
Basis: IFRS 15; IAS 37.
Analysis: Assurance warranty → IAS 37 provision; separately sold extended warranty → a separate performance obligation, allocated price recognised over the warranty term; right of return → refund liability (expected returns) and an asset for the right to recover goods (cost of expected returns) (IFR-061).

IFR-061.q: 100 cases of beverages are sold at 1,000 (VND thousand) per case with a right of return; 5% are expected to be returned. What revenue is recognised (VND thousand)?
IFR-061.e: 100 × 1,000 × 95% = 95,000; 5,000 is recognised as a refund liability.
IFR-061.x:
Basis: IFRS 15 (sales with a right of return – variable consideration).
Working: Revenue = 100 × 1,000 × (1 − 5%) = 95,000 thousand VND; 5,000 thousand is a refund liability. Also record an asset for the right to recover the 5 expected cases at cost (less recovery costs), reducing COGS accordingly.

IFR-062.q: A contract modification adding distinct goods at their standalone selling price is accounted for as a separate contract.
IFR-062.e: True. Other modifications are treated prospectively or by cumulative catch-up.
IFR-062.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraph 20 (contract modifications).
Analysis: True. A modification is a separate contract when both: scope increases with distinct goods or services; and price rises by their standalone selling price. Otherwise: if remaining goods are distinct → treat as terminating the old and creating a new contract (prospective); if not → cumulative catch-up adjustment.

IFR-063.q: Select ALL indicators that control has transferred to the customer at a point in time:
IFR-063.e: Signing a framework agreement does not transfer control.
o: The entity has a present right to payment
The customer has the significant risks and rewards
The customer has accepted the asset
The parties have just signed a framework agreement
IFR-063.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraph 38.
Analysis: Indicators of control transfer at a point in time: (A) a present right to payment; (B) customer's legal title; (C) customer's physical possession; (D) customer bears significant risks and rewards; (E) customer acceptance.
Distractors: (F) A framework agreement creates no specific transfer obligation and passes no control.

IFR-064.q: Distinguish a contract asset from a receivable:
IFR-064.e: Cash received before performance is a contract liability.
o: A receivable is an unconditional right (only time must pass); a contract asset is conditional on something other than time
A contract asset is cash received in advance
A receivable arises only with a VAT invoice
IFR-064.x:
Basis: IFRS 15, paragraphs 105–108.
Analysis: A receivable is an unconditional right to cash (only time must pass); a contract asset is a right to payment for work transferred that still depends on something other than time (e.g., completing the next milestone). Cash received before performance is a contract liability.
Distractors: B and C misdescribe them; D – the right to payment doesn't depend on a VAT invoice.

IFR-065.q: Under IFRS 16, a contract contains a lease when it:
IFR-065.e: Control means the right to obtain substantially all economic benefits and to direct the use.
o: Conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration
IFR-065.x:
Basis: IFRS 16 – Leases, paragraph 9.
Analysis: A contract contains a lease if it conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period in exchange for consideration; control means obtaining substantially all economic benefits and directing the use. An asset is 'identified' if the supplier has no substantive substitution right.
Distractors: B – substance over name; C and D aren't criteria.

IFR-066.q: The lessee accounting model under IFRS 16 is:
IFR-066.e: Except for short-term and low-value exemptions.
o: A single model: recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability for most leases
Straight-line rent expense for all leases
IFR-066.x:
Basis: IFRS 16.
Analysis: Lessees use a single model: a right-of-use (ROU) asset and lease liability for most leases (except short-term and low-value exemptions – IFR-067), with ROU depreciation and interest on the liability.
Distractors: B is the IAS 17/VAS 06 model (still used by lessors – IFR-076); C applies only to exempt leases; D is wrong.

IFR-067.q: Select ALL cases where the lessee may elect an exemption (no ROU asset or lease liability):
IFR-067.e: Long-term land leases with annual payments are still recognised under IFRS 16.
o: Short-term leases (12 months or less, no purchase option)
IFR-067.x:
Basis: IFRS 16, paragraphs 5–8.
Analysis: Optional exemptions: (A) short-term leases – 12 months or less, no purchase option (by asset class); (B) low-value assets when new (e.g., laptops, phones – lease by lease). Payments are expensed straight-line.
Distractors: (C) Long-term land leases paid annually still bring ROU assets and liabilities (IFR-080); (D) VAS classification doesn't decide IFRS treatment.

IFR-068.q: A 3-year vehicle lease with VND 100 million paid at the end of each year; the lessee's incremental borrowing rate is 10%. What is the initial lease liability (VND million, 2 decimals)?
IFR-068.x:
Basis: IFRS 16 (initial measurement of the lease liability).
Working: Liability = PV of payments = 100 × [1 − (1.1)⁻³] / 0.1 = 100 × (1 − 0.751315) / 0.1 = 100 × 2.48685 = 248.69 million VND.
Check by year: 100/1.1 + 100/1.21 + 100/1.331 = 90.91 + 82.64 + 75.13 = 248.68 ≈ 248.69 (rounding).

IFR-069.q: A 3-year car lease pays VND 100 million at each year-end; incremental borrowing rate 10% → initial lease liability VND 248.69 million. Initial direct costs are 10 million with no prepayments. What is the initial right-of-use asset (VND million, 2 decimals)?
IFR-069.e: ROU = lease liability 248.69 + initial direct costs 10 = 258.69 million VND.
IFR-069.x:
Basis: IFRS 16, paragraph 24 (initial measurement of the ROU asset).
Working: ROU = initial liability 248.69 + prepayments 0 + initial direct costs 10 − incentives 0 + estimated restoration costs 0 = 258.69 million VND.

IFR-070.q: A 3-year car lease pays VND 100 million at each year-end; incremental borrowing rate 10%; initial lease liability VND 248.69 million. What is year-1 interest on the lease liability (VND million, 2 decimals)?
IFR-070.x:
Basis: IFRS 16 (effective interest method).
Working: Year-1 interest = opening balance × rate = 248.69 × 10% = 24.87 million VND (Dr interest expense / Cr lease liability).
Note: Interest falls as the balance declines: year 2 = 173.56 × 10% = 17.36; year 3 ≈ 9.09.

IFR-071.q: The right-of-use asset for a 3-year car lease is initially VND 258.69 million, depreciated straight-line over 3 years with no residual value. What is year-1 depreciation (VND million, 2 decimals)?
IFR-071.x:
Basis: IFRS 16; IAS 16 (ROU depreciation).
Working: Year-1 depreciation = 258.69 / 3 = 86.23 million VND.
Note: ROU assets are depreciated over the shorter of lease term and useful life, unless ownership transfers or a purchase option is reasonably certain (then useful life).

IFR-072.q: A 3-year car lease pays VND 100 million at each year-end; rate 10%; initial lease liability VND 248.69 million. What is the lease liability at the end of year 1 (after interest and the 100 million payment) (VND million, 2 decimals)?
IFR-072.x:
Basis: IFRS 16.
Working: Year-end-1 balance = 248.69 + interest 24.87 − payment 100 = 173.56 million VND.
Check: PV of the remaining 2 payments = 100/1.1 + 100/1.21 = 90.91 + 82.64 = 173.55 ≈ 173.56 (rounding).

IFR-073.q: Under IFRS 16, a lessee's total lease-related expense (depreciation + interest) is usually higher in early years than straight-line rent under the old model.
IFR-073.e: True. Interest on a declining balance front-loads the expense.
IFR-073.x:
Basis: IFRS 16.
Analysis: True. From IFR-068–072: year 1 cost = depreciation 86.23 + interest 24.87 = 111.10 > straight-line rent 100; year 3 = 86.23 + 9.09 ≈ 95.32 < 100. Total cost over the term is the same (apart from the 10 million direct costs) but front-loaded, since interest runs on a declining balance.

IFR-074.q: Moving to IFRS 16 usually increases a lessee's EBITDA because rent is replaced by depreciation and interest.
IFR-074.e: True. Analysts must adjust when comparing EBITDA and net debt between VAS and IFRS entities.
IFR-074.x:
Basis: IFRS 16.
Analysis: True. Rent (formerly an operating expense) becomes depreciation + interest – both below EBITDA → EBITDA rises. Net debt also rises (lease liabilities) and operating cash flow rises (principal repayments move to financing).
Note: When comparing EV/EBITDA or debt/EBITDA between VAS and IFRS firms, analysts must put them on the same basis.

IFR-075.q: The discount rate for measuring the lease liability is:
IFR-075.e: The incremental borrowing rate reflects the cost of borrowing to buy a similar asset over a similar term.
o: The interest rate implicit in the lease; if not readily determinable, the lessee's incremental borrowing rate
IFR-075.x:
Basis: IFRS 16, paragraph 26.
Analysis: Discount at the rate implicit in the lease (making PV of payments + unguaranteed residual equal fair value + lessor's direct costs); if not determinable – common for lessees – use the incremental borrowing rate: what the lessee would pay to borrow a similar amount, over a similar term, with similar security.
Distractors: B, C and D don't reflect the lessee's credit risk and term.

IFR-076.q: Under IFRS 16, lessors still classify leases as finance or operating leases.
IFR-076.e: True. Lessor accounting is largely carried over from IAS 17.
IFR-076.x:
Basis: IFRS 16 (lessor accounting).
Analysis: True. Lessors still classify finance leases (substantially all risks and rewards transferred – a lease receivable) or operating leases (asset retained, rental income) – largely as under IAS 17. Hence an asymmetry: the lessee records an ROU asset while the lessor may still carry the asset.

IFR-077.q: Variable rent based on a % of store sales is treated as:
IFR-077.e: Payments varying with an index or rate are included in the liability.
o: Excluded from the lease liability; expensed when incurred
Fully included in the lease liability
IFR-077.x:
Basis: IFRS 16, paragraphs 27–28, 38.
Analysis: Rent varying with store sales depends on future performance → excluded from the lease liability, expensed as incurred. Payments linked to an index (CPI) or rate are included (measured at the commencement index, remeasured when it changes).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.
Note: 'Variable' payments that are in-substance fixed must still be included.

IFR-078.q: Under IFRS 16, the lease term is the non-cancellable period plus:
IFR-078.e: Also periods covered by termination options the lessee is reasonably certain not to exercise.
o: Periods covered by extension options the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise
IFR-078.x:
Basis: IFRS 16, paragraph 18.
Analysis: Lease term = non-cancellable period + periods under extension options the lessee is reasonably certain to exercise + periods under termination options it's reasonably certain not to exercise. Factors: significant leasehold improvements, relocation costs, the asset's importance.
Distractors: B is too broad; C isn't the criterion; D is incomplete.

IFR-079.q: In a sale and leaseback qualifying as a sale under IFRS 15, the seller-lessee recognises only the gain relating to the rights transferred to the buyer-lessor.
IFR-079.e: True. Retained rights are reflected in the ROU asset.
IFR-079.x:
Basis: IFRS 16, paragraphs 98–100 (sale and leaseback).
Analysis: True. If the transfer qualifies as a sale under IFRS 15, the seller-lessee measures the ROU asset at the proportion of the old carrying amount relating to the rights retained, recognising gain or loss only on the rights transferred. If not a sale: keep the asset and record the proceeds as a financial liability (in substance a loan – ACC-104).

IFR-080.q: A Vietnamese company leases land for 30 years with annual payments. On moving to IFRS 16:
IFR-080.e: This can sharply increase assets and liabilities of manufacturers in industrial parks.
o: Recognise a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the present value of payments
Continue annual rent expense as under VAS 06
IFR-080.x:
Basis: IFRS 16; VAS 06.
Analysis: A 30-year land lease paid annually isn't short-term or low-value → recognise an ROU land asset and a lease liability at the PV of payments (discounted at the incremental borrowing rate), with depreciation and interest.
Distractors: B is VAS 06 treatment; C – the business doesn't own the land; D isn't enough.
Note: For manufacturers in industrial parks, total assets and debt may jump, affecting leverage ratios and covenants.

IFR-081.q: A 3-year office lease does not qualify for the IFRS 16 short-term exemption.
IFR-081.e: True. The short-term exemption applies only to lease terms of 12 months or less.
IFR-081.x:
Basis: IFRS 16, Appendix A (short-term lease definition).
Analysis: True. A short-term lease has a term of 12 months or less at commencement and no purchase option. A 3-year office lease exceeds that → an ROU asset and lease liability are required (an office isn't a low-value asset either).

IFR-082.q: Consider these statements on lessee accounting under IFRS 16:
IFR-082.e: Lessees cannot choose the operating model, except for short-term/low-value exemptions.
o: The ROU asset is depreciated over the shorter of lease term and useful life (if ownership does not transfer).
The lease liability is remeasured when the lease term changes.
Lessees may choose the operating lease model for all leases.
ROU assets are presented separately or disclosed.
IFR-082.x:
Basis: IFRS 16.
Analysis: True: ROU depreciation over the shorter of lease term and useful life (no ownership transfer – IFR-071); the liability is remeasured when the term, option assessments or indices change; ROU assets are shown separately or the line items disclosed. False: lessees can't elect operating-lease treatment except for short-term and low-value exemptions (IFR-067).

IFR-083.q: Match the business model and cash flow characteristics with the classification of debt financial assets under IFRS 9:
IFR-083.e: FVTPL may be designated to eliminate an accounting mismatch.
p: Held to collect contractual cash flows, SPPI met
Held to collect and sell, SPPI met
IFR-083.x:
Basis: IFRS 9 – Financial instruments (classifying debt-instrument financial assets).
Analysis: Held to collect contractual cash flows + SPPI → amortised cost; held to collect and sell + SPPI → FVOCI; otherwise (trading, managed on fair value, failing SPPI) → FVTPL.
Note: An FVTPL designation at initial recognition is allowed to eliminate an accounting mismatch.

IFR-084.q: Equity investments not held for trading may be irrevocably designated at FVOCI; cumulative gains/losses are not recycled to profit or loss on sale.
IFR-084.e: True. Dividends are still recognised in profit or loss.
IFR-084.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, paragraph 5.7.5.
Analysis: True. Equity instruments not held for trading may be irrevocably designated (investment by investment) at FVOCI; cumulative OCI gains/losses aren't recycled to P&L on sale – they may only move within equity (to retained earnings). Dividends still go to P&L; there's no impairment test.

IFR-085.q: The SPPI test under IFRS 9 assesses whether:
IFR-085.e: Interest reflects the time value of money, credit risk and a basic lending margin.
o: Contractual cash flows are solely payments of principal and interest on the principal outstanding
The yield is high or low
IFR-085.x:
Basis: IFRS 9 (SPPI test – Solely Payments of Principal and Interest).
Analysis: The SPPI test asks whether contractual cash flows are solely principal and interest on principal outstanding; interest must reflect time value, credit risk, basic lending costs and margin. Returns linked to share or commodity prices → fail SPPI → FVTPL.
Distractors: B, C and D aren't SPPI criteria.

IFR-086.q: Under IFRS 9's general expected credit loss (ECL) model, stage 1 assets carry:
IFR-086.e: Stage 2 (significant increase in credit risk) and stage 3 (credit-impaired) carry lifetime ECL.
IFR-086.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, section 5.5 (general ECL model).
Analysis: Stage 1 – no significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition → 12-month ECL (losses from defaults possible within the next 12 months).
Distractors: B applies to stages 2 and 3; C is wrong – all in-scope assets carry ECL; D has no basis.

IFR-087.q: Match each ECL stage with its features:
IFR-087.e: Staging affects both the allowance and interest income calculation.
p: No significant increase in credit risk – 12-month ECL, interest on gross carrying amount
Significant increase in credit risk – lifetime ECL, interest on gross amount
Credit-impaired – lifetime ECL, interest on net amount
IFR-087.x:
Basis: IFRS 9.
Analysis: Stage 1 – no significant increase: 12-month ECL, interest on gross carrying amount; stage 2 – significant increase: lifetime ECL, interest on gross; stage 3 – credit-impaired: lifetime ECL, interest on net (gross less allowance). Staging affects both the allowance and interest income.

IFR-088.q: A stage-1 loan: exposure (EAD) VND 1,000 million, 12-month PD 2%, LGD 40%. What is the 12-month ECL (VND million)?
IFR-088.x:
Basis: IFRS 9 (ECL measurement).
Working: 12-month ECL = EAD × PD × LGD = 1,000 × 2% × 40% = 8 million VND (ignoring discounting).
Note: In practice ECL is probability-weighted across economic scenarios, forward-looking and discounted at the effective interest rate.

IFR-089.q: For trade receivables without a significant financing component, IFRS 9 requires the simplified approach: always lifetime ECL.
IFR-089.e: True. A provision matrix by ageing, adjusted for forward-looking information, is common.
IFR-089.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, paragraph 5.5.15 (simplified approach).
Analysis: True. For trade receivables and contract assets without a significant financing component, IFRS 9 requires the simplified approach: always lifetime ECL, no stage tracking. Common practice: an ageing-based provision matrix from historical losses adjusted for forward-looking information (IFR-090).
Note: Unlike Circular 48/2019, which provides only from 6 months overdue (ACC-050).

IFR-090.q: Provision matrix: current receivables VND 1,000 million (1%), 1–30 days overdue 500 million (5%), over 90 days 100 million (50%). What is the ECL allowance (VND million)?
IFR-090.x:
Basis: IFRS 9 (provision matrix).
Working: Not due 1,000 × 1% = 10; 1–30 days 500 × 5% = 25; over 90 days 100 × 50% = 50. Total allowance = 10 + 25 + 50 = 85 million VND.
Note: Under IFRS 9 even not-yet-due balances carry an allowance – a key difference from Circular 48/2019.

IFR-091.q: IFRS 9 contains a rebuttable presumption that credit risk has increased significantly when payments are more than 30 days past due.
IFR-091.e: True. More than 90 days past due is a rebuttable presumption of default.
IFR-091.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, paragraph 5.5.11.
Analysis: True. Rebuttable presumption: credit risk has increased significantly when payments are over 30 days past due (stage 2), unless reasonable and supportable information shows otherwise. Over 90 days is the rebuttable default presumption (stage 3 – IFR-092). Entities should use forward-looking information, not wait for arrears.

IFR-092.q: Under IFRS 9, the rebuttable presumption of default applies when payments are past due by more than:
IFR-092.e: It can be rebutted with reasonable and supportable information.
IFR-092.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, paragraph B5.5.37.
Analysis: The rebuttable presumption is that default occurs no later than 90 days past due, unless reasonable and supportable information shows a longer criterion is more appropriate.
Distractors: B is the significant-increase presumption (IFR-091); C and D aren't the standard's thresholds.

IFR-093.q: A bond is bought for VND 950 million (amortised cost), coupon 50 million per year, effective interest rate 7%. What is year-1 interest income (VND million)?
IFR-093.x:
Basis: IFRS 9 (effective interest method).
Working: Year-1 interest income = opening amortised cost × effective rate = 950 × 7% = 66.5 million VND.
Note: It differs from the 50 million coupon; the 16.5 million gap is discount amortisation (IFR-094).

IFR-094.q: A bond at amortised cost is bought for VND 950 million; coupon received 50 million per year; effective rate 7%. What is the amortised cost at the end of year 1 (VND million)?
IFR-094.x:
Basis: IFRS 9.
Working: Amortised cost at end of year 1 = 950 + effective interest 66.5 − coupon received 50 = 966.5 million VND.
Note: Amortised cost accretes toward par (assume 1,000) by maturity as the discount unwinds.

IFR-095.e: Fair value is an exit price from a market perspective.
o: The price received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date
IFR-095.x:
Basis: IFRS 13 – Fair value measurement.
Analysis: Fair value is the price received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date – an exit price from a market, not entity-specific, perspective.
Distractors: B is a historical entry price; C is entity-specific (e.g., IAS 36 value in use); D lacks objectivity.

IFR-096.q: Match each IFRS 13 fair value hierarchy level with its inputs:
IFR-096.e: Level 3 requires more disclosure and carries higher audit risk.
p: Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets
Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices
IFR-096.x:
Basis: IFRS 13 (fair value hierarchy).
Analysis: Level 1 – unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets (liquid listed shares); Level 2 – other observable inputs (similar assets' prices, rates, yield curves); Level 3 – unobservable inputs (internal cash-flow forecasts for unlisted equity).
Note: Level 3 needs movement reconciliations and sensitivity disclosures and is a high audit-risk area (VSA-079).

IFR-097.q: The 'highest and best use' concept in IFRS 13 applies to fair value measurement of non-financial assets.
IFR-097.e: True. E.g., land used as a warehouse that could be redeveloped for housing.
IFR-097.x:
Basis: IFRS 13, paragraphs 27–30.
Analysis: True. Fair value of non-financial assets rests on 'highest and best use' by market participants – physically possible, legally permissible, financially feasible – even if the entity uses it differently. E.g., land used as a warehouse but zoned for higher-value housing → valued for housing (less conversion costs).

IFR-098.q: An entity uses a forward to hedge FX risk on a highly probable forecast USD purchase of components in 3 months. The appropriate hedge accounting type:
IFR-098.e: Highly probable forecast transactions are cash flow hedge items.
IFR-098.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, Chapter 6 (hedge accounting).
Analysis: The hedged item is a highly probable forecast transaction (a USD component purchase in 3 months) – FX moves affect future cash flows → cash flow hedge.
Distractors: B is for recognised items or unrecognised firm commitments; C for net investments in foreign operations; D is wrong if designation, documentation and effectiveness criteria are met.

IFR-099.q: In a cash flow hedge, the effective portion of the hedging instrument's gain/loss is recognised in OCI (cash flow hedge reserve).
IFR-099.e: True. The ineffective portion goes to profit or loss.
IFR-099.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, paragraph 6.5.11.
Analysis: True. In a cash flow hedge, the effective portion of the hedging instrument's gain/loss goes to OCI (cash flow hedge reserve); ineffectiveness goes to P&L. When the forecast transaction occurs, the reserve moves into the cost of a non-financial asset (e.g., inventory) or to P&L when the hedged item affects it.

IFR-100.q: Under IAS 32, preference shares with mandatory redemption on a fixed date are classified as:
IFR-100.e: A contractual obligation to deliver cash → liability, regardless of legal form.
IFR-100.x:
Basis: IAS 32 – Financial instruments: Presentation.
Analysis: Mandatorily redeemable preference shares create a contractual obligation to deliver cash the entity can't avoid → a financial liability, whatever the legal label (substance over form – ACC-104). Their dividends are recognised as interest expense.
Distractors: B applies only if the entity has an unconditional right to avoid paying; C and D are wrong.

IFR-101.q: Convertible bonds (compound instruments) are split into liability and equity components.
IFR-101.e: True under IAS 32: the liability is measured at present value; the residual is equity.
IFR-101.x:
Basis: IAS 32 (compound financial instruments).
Analysis: True. A convertible bond (fixed number of shares) combines a principal-and-interest obligation (liability) and a conversion right (equity). The liability is the PV of cash flows at the rate on a similar non-convertible bond; the residual proceeds are equity.

IFR-102.q: An entity sells receivables to a bank under full-recourse factoring. Under IFRS 9:
IFR-102.e: The entity retains substantially all risks and rewards, so no derecognition.
o: Continue recognising the receivables and recognise a borrowing
IFR-102.x:
Basis: IFRS 9, section 3.2 (derecognition of financial assets).
Analysis: Full-recourse factoring: the entity still bears customer default risk → retains substantially all risks and rewards → the receivable isn't derecognised; bank proceeds are a secured borrowing.
Distractors: B applies only when substantially all risks and rewards transfer (non-recourse factoring); C and D are wrong.

IFR-103.q: The 2024 amendments to IFRS 9 and IFRS 7 on classification and measurement are effective for annual periods beginning on or after 01/01/2026.
IFR-103.e: True. They cover derecognising liabilities settled via electronic payment and SPPI assessment of ESG-linked features.
IFR-103.x:
Basis: Amendments to IFRS 9 and IFRS 7 – Classification and Measurement of Financial Instruments (IASB, May 2024).
Analysis: True. Effective for annual periods beginning on or after 01/01/2026 (early adoption permitted). Content: an option to derecognise liabilities settled via electronic payment systems before settlement date (if conditions are met); SPPI guidance for ESG-linked features; more disclosures on FVOCI equity and contingent features.

IFR-104.q: 1,000 listed shares are bought at VND 20,000 and classified as FVTPL; the year-end price is 23,000. What gain is recognised in profit or loss (VND million)?
IFR-104.x:
Basis: IFRS 9 (FVTPL).
Working: Gain = 1,000 × (23,000 − 20,000) = 3,000,000 VND = 3 million VND, to P&L.
Note: Under VAS/Circular 48, trading securities get allowances only for declines; unrealised gains aren't recognised – a big conversion difference.

IFR-105.q: After initial recognition, IAS 16 permits measuring PP&E using:
IFR-105.e: VAS 03 allows only cost (revaluation only when required by the State).
o: The cost model or the revaluation model (applied to the entire class)
Fair value through profit or loss only
Prices set by the tax authority
IFR-105.x:
Basis: IAS 16; VAS 03.
Analysis: IAS 16 allows the cost model (cost − depreciation − impairment) or the revaluation model (fair value at revaluation − subsequent depreciation and impairment), applied to entire asset classes with sufficient regularity.
Distractors: B is VAS 03 (revaluation only when the State requires); C and D have no basis.

IFR-106.q: A factory with a carrying amount of VND 800 billion is revalued to 1,000 billion (first revaluation). What revaluation surplus is recognised in OCI (VND billion)?
IFR-106.x:
Basis: IAS 16 (revaluation model).
Working: Surplus = 1,000 − 800 = 200 billion VND to OCI (revaluation surplus in equity), before deferred tax.
Note: A deferred tax liability on the 200 billion (IAS 12) also goes to OCI; later decreases first reduce the surplus, any excess goes to P&L (IFR-126).

IFR-107.q: IAS 16 requires separate depreciation of significant parts of PP&E with different useful lives (component depreciation).
IFR-107.e: True. E.g., aircraft engines are depreciated separately from the airframe.
IFR-107.x:
Basis: IAS 16, paragraphs 43–47.
Analysis: True. Each part with cost significant to the whole and a different useful life is depreciated separately (aircraft engines, blast-furnace linings, factory roofs). On replacement, the new part is capitalised and the old one derecognised. A worked example is IFR-153.

IFR-108.e: Development-phase costs are capitalised once all criteria are met.
IFR-108.x:
Basis: IAS 38 – Intangible assets, paragraph 54.
Analysis: Research-phase costs are expensed as incurred – future benefits can't yet be shown. Development-phase costs are capitalised once all 6 criteria are met (as in VAS 04 – ACC-106).
Distractors: B, C and D have no basis.

IFR-109.q: A new management software development project: VND 300 million spent before meeting the capitalisation criteria, 500 million after. How much is capitalised (VND million)?
IFR-109.e: Only costs after meeting the criteria are capitalised; the 300 million expensed cannot be reinstated.
IFR-109.x:
Basis: IAS 38, paragraphs 65 and 71.
Working: Only costs from the date all criteria are met are capitalised = 500 million VND. The earlier 300 million was expensed and can't be reinstated as an asset later.

IFR-110.q: Internally generated brands and customer lists are not recognised as intangible assets under IAS 38.
IFR-110.e: True. Brands acquired in a business combination are recognised at fair value.
IFR-110.x:
Basis: IAS 38, paragraphs 63–64; IFRS 3.
Analysis: True. Internally generated brands, customer lists and mastheads aren't recognised, since their costs can't be separated from developing the business as a whole. Conversely, brands and customer lists acquired in a business combination are recognised separately at acquisition-date fair value.

IFR-111.q: Under IAS 36, an asset's recoverable amount is:
IFR-111.e: Impairment = carrying amount − recoverable amount (if positive).
o: The higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use
IFR-111.x:
Basis: IAS 36 – Impairment of assets.
Analysis: Recoverable amount = the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use (PV of expected cash flows from continued use). The higher is used because the entity would choose the better option (sell or use). Impairment = carrying amount − recoverable amount (if positive).
Distractors: B is reversed; C and D aren't the definition.

IFR-112.q: A production line has a carrying amount of VND 500 billion; fair value less costs of disposal 420 billion; value in use 450 billion. What is the impairment loss (VND billion)?
IFR-112.e: Recoverable amount = max(420; 450) = 450; impairment = 500 − 450 = 50 billion VND.
IFR-112.x:
Basis: IAS 36.
Working: Recoverable amount = max(420; 450) = 450 billion. Impairment = 500 − 450 = 50 billion VND, to P&L (unless under the revaluation model – then first against the surplus).

IFR-113.q: Goodwill must be tested for impairment annually; impairment losses on goodwill are never reversed.
IFR-113.x:
Basis: IAS 36, paragraphs 90 and 124.
Analysis: True. Goodwill isn't amortised and is tested for impairment at least annually (and on indicators) at the cash-generating unit level it's allocated to. Goodwill impairment can't be reversed – a later recovery may be internally generated goodwill, which isn't recognised.

IFR-114.q: Which external indicator suggests possible impairment under IAS 36?
IFR-114.e: Other indicators: rising market rates, adverse technological or legal changes; obsolescence or damage.
o: The entity's market capitalisation is below its net assets
IFR-114.x:
Basis: IAS 36, paragraph 12 (impairment indicators).
Analysis: External indicator: market capitalisation below net assets – the market values the entity below book; also rising market rates (lowering value in use), adverse technological, market or legal changes; internal: obsolescence, damage, worse-than-expected performance.
Distractors: B and D are positive signs; C – falling rates increase value in use.

IFR-115.q: Under IAS 2, inventories are measured at:
o: The lower of cost and net realisable value
IFR-115.x:
Basis: IAS 2 – Inventories.
Analysis: Inventory is measured at the lower of cost and NRV (estimated selling price − costs to complete − costs to sell) – as in VAS 02 (ACC-029).
Distractors: B and C aren't measurement bases; D ignores write-downs when NRV is below cost.

IFR-116.q: IAS 2 does not permit the last-in, first-out (LIFO) method.
IFR-116.e: True. Only FIFO, weighted average or specific identification are allowed.
IFR-116.x:
Basis: IAS 2, paragraph 25.
Analysis: True. IAS 2 (revised 2003) bans LIFO because it leaves balance-sheet inventory at outdated prices, unfaithful when prices move. Only FIFO, weighted average and specific identification (for non-interchangeable items) are allowed. Vietnam also dropped LIFO from Circular 200/2014 (ACC-027).

IFR-117.q: A lot costs VND 100 million; estimated selling price 95 million; estimated costs to sell 5 million. What is the inventory write-down (VND million)?
IFR-117.x:
Basis: IAS 2.
Working: NRV = 95 − 5 = 90 million. Cost 100 > NRV 90 → write-down = 100 − 90 = 10 million VND (expensed – usually COGS).
Note: If NRV recovers later, the write-down is reversed up to the amount written down.

IFR-118.q: Under IAS 40, investment property after initial recognition is measured using:
IFR-118.e: Under the fair value model, no depreciation is charged.
o: The fair value model (changes in profit or loss) or the cost model
IFR-118.x:
Basis: IAS 40 – Investment property.
Analysis: After initial recognition, choose the fair value model (changes to P&L, no depreciation) or the cost model (as IAS 16, with fair value disclosed), for all investment property.
Distractors: B is VAS 05 (ACC-122); C – fair value changes don't go to OCI; D – provincial land price tables aren't fair value.

IFR-119.q: Investment property under the fair value model is not depreciated.
IFR-119.e: True. Fair value changes flow through profit or loss, making earnings more volatile.
IFR-119.x:
Basis: IAS 40, paragraphs 33–35.
Analysis: True. Under the fair value model, investment property is remeasured each period with changes in P&L – no depreciation. Profit becomes more volatile with the property market; investors should strip out (non-cash) revaluation gains when analysing core earnings.

IFR-120.q: Under IAS 41, livestock held for produce (e.g., dairy cattle, sheep for wool) is measured at:
IFR-120.e: Unless fair value cannot be measured reliably on initial recognition.
o: Fair value less costs to sell, with changes in profit or loss
The selling price of harvested produce
IFR-120.x:
Basis: IAS 41 – Agriculture.
Analysis: Biological assets (producing animals like dairy cows, wool sheep) are measured at fair value less costs to sell at initial recognition and each reporting date; changes go to P&L. Exception: if fair value can't be measured reliably at initial recognition → cost less depreciation and impairment.
Distractors: B applies only to bearer plants (IFR-121); C and D are wrong.

IFR-121.q: Bearer plants such as coffee and rubber trees are accounted for under IAS 16; produce growing on them remains under IAS 41.
IFR-121.x:
Basis: IAS 16; IAS 41 (2014 amendments – bearer plants).
Analysis: True. Bearer plants (coffee, rubber, tea, oil palm) are used only to bear produce over several periods, like machinery → accounted as PP&E under IAS 16 (cost or revaluation). Produce growing on them (unharvested coffee cherries) stays under IAS 41 at fair value less costs to sell.

IFR-122.q: Dairy cows are 'bearer animals' and so are accounted for under IAS 16 like bearer plants.
IFR-122.e: False. The IAS 16 exception covers only bearer plants; bearer animals remain under IAS 41.
IFR-122.x:
Basis: IAS 41; IAS 16.
Analysis: False. The IAS 16 exception covers only plants (bearer plants); producing animals (dairy cows, laying hens) stay under IAS 41 at fair value less costs to sell. The IASB's reasoning: animals have more active markets and undergo significant biological transformation over their lives.

IFR-123.q: A herd of 100 head of livestock has fair value of VND 30 million each and costs to sell of 1 million each. The opening value was 2,700 million (no purchases or sales). What gain is recognised in profit or loss (VND million)?
IFR-123.x:
Basis: IAS 41.
Working: Closing value = 100 × (30 − 1) = 2,900 million. Gain = 2,900 − 2,700 = 200 million VND, to P&L.
Note: The gain combines physical growth and price changes; IAS 41 encourages disclosing them separately.

IFR-124.q: Coffee cherries just harvested from a coffee plantation are agricultural produce; under IAS 41 they are measured:
IFR-124.e: Harvest is the hand-off point from IAS 41 to IAS 2.
o: At fair value less costs to sell at the point of harvest; thereafter as inventory cost under IAS 2
IFR-124.x:
Basis: IAS 41, paragraph 13; IAS 2.
Analysis: Agricultural produce at harvest is measured at fair value less costs to sell (IAS 41); that becomes its cost as inventory under IAS 2 thereafter. Harvest is the boundary between IAS 41 and IAS 2.
Distractors: B, C and D don't match the standards.

IFR-125.q: Under IAS 23, borrowing costs directly attributable to constructing a qualifying asset are:
IFR-125.e: Similar to VAS 16; capitalisation stops when the asset is ready for use.
IFR-125.x:
Basis: IAS 23 – Borrowing costs.
Analysis: Borrowing costs directly attributable to acquiring, constructing or producing a qualifying asset (needing substantial time to get ready) must be capitalised (IAS 23 allows no expensing choice); capitalisation stops when the asset is substantially ready. Similar to VAS 16 (ACC-100).
Distractors: B, C and D are wrong.

IFR-126.q: Consider these statements on asset accounting under IFRS:
o: A revaluation decrease below cost (no prior surplus) goes to profit or loss.
Intangibles with indefinite useful lives are not amortised but tested for impairment annually.
Value in use under IAS 36 uses a pre-tax discount rate.
IFR-126.x:
Basis: IAS 16; IAS 38; IAS 36; IAS 2.
Analysis: True: a revaluation decrease below cost with no prior surplus → P&L; indefinite-life intangibles aren't amortised and are tested annually; IAS 36 value in use uses a pre-tax discount rate. False: IAS 2 bans LIFO (IFR-116).

IFR-127.q: Under IFRS 10, an investor controls an investee when it has all of:
IFR-127.e: Control rests on substance, not just ownership percentage.
o: Power over the investee, exposure/rights to variable returns, and the ability to use power to affect returns
More than 50% ownership in all cases
IFR-127.x:
Basis: IFRS 10 – Consolidated FS, paragraph 7.
Analysis: An investor controls when it has all three: (1) power over the investee (current ability to direct relevant activities); (2) exposure or rights to variable returns; (3) the ability to use power to affect those returns. Control rests on substance, not just ownership percentage.
Distractors: B is too mechanical (IFR-128); C and D aren't enough.

IFR-128.q: Under IFRS 10, an investor may control an investee with less than 50% of voting rights (de facto control).
IFR-128.e: True. E.g., holding 45% while the rest is widely dispersed.
IFR-128.x:
Basis: IFRS 10, paragraphs B41–B46 (less than a majority of voting rights).
Analysis: True. An investor holding under 50% may have de facto control when its stake is large relative to dispersed others (e.g., 45% with the rest held by thousands of small holders) and voting patterns show it always prevails; or via contracts or substantive potential voting rights.

IFR-129.q: 80% of a subsidiary is acquired for VND 1,000 billion; fair value of identifiable net assets 900 billion; NCI measured at its proportionate share. What is goodwill (VND billion)?
IFR-129.x:
Basis: IFRS 3 – Business combinations.
Working: NCI (proportionate share) = 20% × 900 = 180 billion. Goodwill = consideration 1,000 + NCI 180 − identifiable net assets 900 = 280 billion VND.
Check: parent's share = 1,000 − 80% × 900 = 1,000 − 720 = 280.

IFR-130.q: Under IFRS 3, non-controlling interest at the acquisition date may be measured at:
o: Fair value or the proportionate share of identifiable net assets
IFR-130.x:
Basis: IFRS 3, paragraph 19.
Analysis: At acquisition, NCI (present ownership interests entitling holders to net assets on liquidation) is measured, transaction by transaction, at: (1) fair value → 'full' goodwill (including NCI's share); or (2) the proportionate share of identifiable net assets → goodwill for the parent's share only (IFR-129).
Distractors: B, C and D have no basis.

IFR-131.q: A bargain purchase gain is recognised in profit or loss after the acquirer reassesses the identification and measurement of assets and liabilities.
IFR-131.x:
Basis: IFRS 3, paragraphs 34–36.
Analysis: True. When identifiable net assets exceed consideration (a bargain purchase – often a forced sale), the acquirer first reassesses whether all assets and liabilities are identified and correctly measured; any remaining excess is a gain in P&L at the acquisition date.

IFR-132.q: Advisory and legal costs of a business combination under IFRS 3 are:
IFR-132.x:
Basis: IFRS 3, paragraph 53.
Analysis: Acquisition-related costs (advisory, legal, accounting, valuation, finder's fees) are expensed as incurred – they aren't part of the exchange for the acquiree. Costs of issuing debt or equity to fund the deal follow IFRS 9/IAS 32 (reducing the liability or equity).
Distractors: B was the old IFRS 3 (2004) treatment and VAS 11's; C and D are wrong.

IFR-133.q: Under IAS 28, holding 20% or more of voting power (directly or indirectly) is presumed to give significant influence; the investment is accounted for using:
IFR-133.e: The presumption can be rebutted if significant influence is shown to be absent.
IFR-133.x:
Basis: IAS 28 – Investments in associates and joint ventures.
Analysis: Holding 20% or more of votes (directly or indirectly) presumes significant influence – participation in financial and operating policy without control → equity method (IFR-134). The presumption can be rebutted if no significant influence is shown.
Distractors: B is for subsidiaries; C and D aren't required for associates.

IFR-134.q: VND 300 billion is invested for 30% of an associate. During the year the associate earns 100 billion and pays total dividends of 20 billion. What is the year-end carrying amount under the equity method (VND billion)?
IFR-134.x:
Basis: IAS 28 (equity method).
Working: Closing carrying amount = cost 300 + share of profit 30% × 100 − dividends received 30% × 20 = 300 + 30 − 6 = 324 billion VND.
Note: Dividends reduce the investment rather than being income – the share of profit was already recognised when the associate earned it.

IFR-135.q: Under IFRS 11, a joint venturer accounts for its interest using:
IFR-135.e: A joint operator recognises its share of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses.
o: Its share of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses
IFR-135.x:
Basis: IFRS 11 – Joint arrangements.
Analysis: A joint venture – parties have rights to the arrangement's net assets → equity method (IAS 28).
Distractors: B is the treatment for a joint operation – parties have rights to specific assets and obligations for liabilities; C is for subsidiaries; D doesn't apply in consolidated FS.

IFR-136.q: Under IAS 12, deferred tax arises from:
IFR-136.e: Taxable temporary differences create deferred tax liabilities; deductible ones create deferred tax assets.
o: Temporary differences between the carrying amount and tax base of assets and liabilities
IFR-136.x:
Basis: IAS 12 – Income taxes.
Analysis: Deferred tax arises from temporary differences between carrying amounts and tax bases of assets and liabilities: taxable differences → deferred tax liabilities; deductible differences and unused tax losses → deferred tax assets (as in VAS 17 – ACC-031).
Distractors: B – permanent differences create no deferred tax; C and D are unrelated.

IFR-137.q: Machinery has a carrying amount of VND 1,000 million and a tax base of 800 million; tax rate 20%. What is the deferred tax liability (VND million)?
IFR-137.x:
Basis: IAS 12.
Working: Taxable temporary difference = 1,000 − 800 = 200 million. Deferred tax liability = 200 × 20% = 40 million VND.
Note: Carrying amount > tax base (often due to faster tax depreciation) → recovering the asset will produce more taxable income than accounting profit.

IFR-138.q: A deferred tax asset for unused tax losses is recognised only to the extent it is probable that future taxable profit will be available.
IFR-138.e: True. A history of recent losses is strong contrary evidence.
IFR-138.x:
Basis: IAS 12, paragraphs 34–36.
Analysis: True. Deferred tax assets from unused losses and credits are recognised only to the extent it's probable that future taxable profit will be available. Recent losses are strong contrary evidence – then convincing other evidence is needed (enough taxable temporary differences, feasible tax planning).
Note: In Vietnam, losses carry forward for at most 5 years (CIT) – limiting utilisation.

IFR-139.q: IAS 12 has a mandatory temporary exception: no recognition or disclosure of deferred tax related to Pillar Two income taxes (global minimum tax).
IFR-139.e: True. Entities still disclose current Pillar Two tax expense and expected exposure.
IFR-139.x:
Basis: Amendments to IAS 12 – International Tax Reform: Pillar Two Model Rules (IASB, May 2023).
Analysis: True. A mandatory temporary exception: no recognition or disclosure of deferred tax assets and liabilities related to Pillar Two income taxes (the 15% global minimum tax). Entities must still disclose that they applied it, current Pillar Two tax expense and information on exposure (cf. Resolution 107/2023/QH15 – FCT-084, ACC-021).

IFR-140.q: Under IAS 37, a provision is recognised when:
